question: Do common image classifiers operate by interpolation once their last-hidden-layer activities are mapped into a low-dimensional autoencoder latent space, and is local distance to the training set more closely related to test correctness than convex-hull membership?

key_findings.claim: A small autoencoder bottleneck often preserves the endpoint classification accuracy of the frozen MNIST and CIFAR-10 classifiers studied in the paper.
key_findings.evidence: The probe reconstructs the 128-dimensional last hidden activity through bottlenecks of 2, 4, 8, or 16 dimensions and feeds the reconstruction into the unchanged output layer. Figure 4 reports that 4 or 8 bottleneck dimensions are generally sufficient for the hybrid network to reach the base network's test accuracy across three MLP widths and three CNN depths, averaged over ten initializations. This is useful evidence that the final decision can be supported by a compact reconstructive code in these simple models; it does not by itself identify the manifold dimension.

anchors.section: Sections 2.1-2.3, probe definition and toy validation

key_findings.claim: Classification preservation through a bottleneck is not a valid estimator of the true intrinsic dimension without additional identifiability and geometry checks.
key_findings.evidence: The stopping rule is the test classification plateau of a frozen output head, not reconstruction error or recovery of local manifold dimension. A nonlinear autoencoder can discard decision-irrelevant variation, so a 4- or 8-dimensional sufficient code may be smaller than the activity manifold. Even the toy ambiguously controls dimension: class centers occupy an author-designated low-dimensional subspace embedded in 32D, but samples are described as having isotropic Gaussian variance around those 32D centers. If that covariance is full-rank, the distributions have full 32D support and only the discriminative center subspace has the designated dimension. No code or covariance-rank statement resolves this. The four coarse bottlenecks and absent geometry checks therefore do not identify true intrinsic dimension.

anchors.section: Section 2.3, bottleneck candidates and MSE training

key_findings.claim: The conclusion that the networks 'actually' interpolate is not representation-invariant and is contradicted by the paper's own motivating geometry.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 explicitly demonstrates that a nonlinear activity map can move every test point from inside a training convex hull to outside it. The learned autoencoder encoder is another nonlinear coordinate map, and its latent chart is nonidentifiable: alternative nonlinear reparameterizations can preserve decoder reconstructions and classifier outputs while changing convex-hull membership. Convex-hull membership is invariant under invertible affine transformations, not arbitrary nonlinear ones. Measuring a large in-hull fraction in one learned chart therefore cannot establish an intrinsic operating regime or refute the high-dimensional result; it shows precisely that the interpolation label depends on the chosen representation.

key_findings.claim: Nearest-neighbor distance is associated with correctness in many reported settings, but this association does not diagnose interpolation as the prediction mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 and Supplementary Figures S1-S12 compare Euclidean, correct-class Euclidean, and cosine nearest-neighbor distances in neural and 16-dimensional latent spaces for all four dataset/architecture combinations. Correct predictions are often closer to training samples, and distance frequently has a larger logistic z-value than hull membership, although the paper notes divergences for poorly performing CIFAR-10 MLPs. Errors are generally more common in sparse, ambiguous, or boundary regions for interpolative, extrapolative, and Bayes-optimal rules alike. Correct-class distance also uses the test label and can align mechanically with correct classification. These plots support proximity as an error correlate, not the stronger claim that the network computes local interpolation.

key_findings.claim: Comparing logistic-regression z-values does not establish that distance contributes more predictive information than hull membership.
key_findings.evidence: The fitted model is accuracy ~ distance + in_hull + distance:in_hull, and the paper interprets coefficient z-values as showing the 'main contribution' comes from distance. A z-value is a significance statistic, not incremental importance. In this interaction model, main effects are conditional at distance=0 or outside the hull, and collinearity, centering/parameterization, sample size, and repeated-example dependence undermine raw cross-predictor comparison. Simple multiplicative feature scaling is not itself a valid objection because coefficient and standard error rescale together in an unpenalized GLM. The same benchmark examples are reused across ten models, so a defensible comparison needs cross-validated likelihood, calibration, or discrimination changes with clustered uncertainty.

key_findings.claim: The claimed inverse relationship between model quality and intrinsic dimension is a coarse architecture correlation rather than an isolated effect.
key_findings.evidence: The study compares only three first-layer widths per MLP and three block depths per CNN. Width or depth changes capacity and optimization jointly with accuracy, and the inferred dimension is selected from only 2, 4, 8, or 16. Figure 4 has no matched-accuracy controls, preregistered dimension threshold, formal regression, or estimator uncertainty. In particular, CIFAR-10 MLP accuracy ranges only from 52.7% to 56.9%, while CIFAR CNN depth changes accuracy from 74.4% to 87.7%; these heterogeneous model families cannot isolate accuracy as the cause of lower estimated dimension.

key_findings.claim: The convex-hull results are not computationally reproducible from the paper or its current public artifacts.
key_findings.evidence: The paper specifies no hull-membership algorithm, feasibility formulation, numerical tolerance, conditioning rule, normalization, or failure handling for testing up to benchmark-scale sample sets in as many as 16 latent dimensions. The text says code 'will be made available on GitHub,' while the exact source leaves a commented placeholder URL ending in /TODO. The official source archive contains TeX, bibliography, and rendered plot files but no scripts, seeds, raw arrays, checkpoints, or environment. As of 2026-08-24 the author's public GitHub account has six repositories, none for this paper, so neither the hull computation nor any paper result can be regenerated from an official artifact.

anchors.section: Section 2.3, technical details and code statement

key_findings.claim: The empirical scope cannot support broad claims about neural-network extrapolation or a stark contrast with human generalization.
key_findings.evidence: All real-data experiments use MNIST or CIFAR-10, simple MLPs or small CNNs, and only the final 128-unit hidden layer. The test sets are standard in-distribution held-out examples; there is no distribution shift, compositional or systematic extrapolation split, intervention on distance, modern architecture, representation-layer sweep, or human experiment. Concluding that artificial networks broadly face difficulty outside a local training neighborhood and contrast sharply with human subjects therefore goes beyond the evaluated tasks and models.

method.core_idea: Train a nonlinear autoencoder on final-hidden-layer activities, use bottleneck classification preservation as a proxy for intrinsic dimension, and measure convex-hull membership and nearest-neighbor proximity in the resulting latent space.
method.mechanism: Train MNIST and CIFAR-10 MLP or CNN classifiers whose last hidden layer has width 128. Freeze each classifier, train a 128-256-bottleneck-256-128 reconstruction autoencoder on training activities with bottleneck sizes 2, 4, 8, and 16, replace the hidden activity by its reconstruction, and compare hybrid test accuracy with the original. Compute the fraction of test latent codes in the training-code convex hull. At 16 dimensions, relate correctness to hull membership and Euclidean, correct-class Euclidean, or cosine nearest-neighbor distance using binned accuracy, conditional means, Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics, and logistic regression over ten random initializations.
assumptions: Preserving frozen-head test classification is sufficient to identify the true intrinsic dimension of hidden activities.
The trained autoencoder latent coordinates preserve the geometry relevant to interpolation and proximity.
Convex-hull membership in one nonlinear latent chart represents a property of the network rather than a coordinate-dependent diagnostic.
The four candidate bottleneck sizes are fine enough to locate a meaningful dimension threshold.
The linear-rotation Gaussian toy validates the estimator for nonlinear real-data representation manifolds.
Nearest-neighbor distance can distinguish an interpolative mechanism from density, ambiguity, margin, or representation-quality effects.
Coefficient z-values in a correlated logistic model provide a valid comparison of predictor contributions.
Ten model initializations and bootstrap intervals adequately characterize uncertainty despite reuse of the same benchmark examples.
Changing MLP width or CNN depth provides a suitable proxy for changing model quality while leaving relevant confounders controlled.
Standard in-distribution classification behavior supports conclusions about extrapolation and human-like generalization.

techniques.role: Maps 128-dimensional final-hidden-layer activities through a learned low-dimensional bottleneck and reconstructs them.
Feeds reconstructed activities into the frozen classifier head to measure decision preservation.
Uses candidate latent widths 2, 4, 8, and 16 as a coarse dimension probe.
Labels test codes as interpolating when they fall in the convex hull of training codes.
Measures Euclidean, ground-truth-class Euclidean, and cosine proximity to training examples in neural and latent spaces.
Regresses correctness on distance, hull membership, and their interaction and compares coefficient z-values.
Uses the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic to compare nearest-neighbor-distance distributions for correct and incorrect predictions.

evaluations.setting: Ten Gaussian classes with controlled intrinsic dimension, orthogonally embedded in 32 dimensions; 5,000 training and 1,000 test samples per class
evaluations.metric: Hybrid-to-base relative classification accuracy across bottleneck dimensions
evaluations.result: Across ten trials with mean absolute accuracy 71%, relative accuracy reaches the base model at the author-designated discriminative center-subspace dimension and then plateaus; the full support dimension is ambiguous under the stated isotropic noise
evaluations.baseline: Frozen one-hidden-layer 32-unit MLP evaluated without the autoencoder

evaluations.setting: MNIST and CIFAR-10 with three-hidden-layer MLPs whose first width is 64, 256, or 1,024
evaluations.metric: Relative test accuracy and fraction of test latent codes within the training convex hull at bottleneck widths 2, 4, 8, and 16
evaluations.result: Figure 4 reports near-base accuracy by 4 or 8 dimensions and mostly high in-hull fractions at low bottleneck dimension; base accuracies are 97.9%-98.5% on MNIST and 52.7%-56.9% on CIFAR-10
evaluations.baseline: Each original frozen MLP at the same initialization

evaluations.setting: MNIST and CIFAR-10 with CNNs containing one, two, or three repeated two-convolution/max-pooling blocks
evaluations.metric: Relative test accuracy and fraction of test latent codes within the training convex hull at bottleneck widths 2, 4, 8, and 16
evaluations.result: Figure 4 reports near-base accuracy by 4 or 8 dimensions and decreasing in-hull fraction as dimension grows; base accuracies are 99.3%-99.6% on MNIST and 74.4%-87.7% on CIFAR-10
evaluations.baseline: Each original frozen CNN at the same initialization

evaluations.setting: MNIST MLPs in original 128-dimensional neural space and the 16-dimensional learned latent space
evaluations.metric: Accuracy by Euclidean nearest-neighbor-distance decile, conditional distance, logistic coefficient z-values, and KS distance
evaluations.result: Figure 5 reports declining accuracy with distance and a more consistently large distance coefficient than hull coefficient across the three widths
evaluations.baseline: Convex-hull membership and its interaction with distance in the same logistic model

evaluations.setting: All MNIST/CIFAR-10 and MLP/CNN combinations at 16 latent dimensions
evaluations.metric: Euclidean, ground-truth-class Euclidean, and cosine nearest-neighbor analyses
evaluations.result: Figures S1-S12 mostly reproduce the association between smaller distance and correct prediction, while the authors explicitly note divergent distance behavior for some poorly performing CIFAR-10 MLP cases
evaluations.baseline: Hull membership under the same autoencoder chart

limitations: A classifier-preserving bottleneck measures a sufficient decision code, not necessarily the intrinsic dimension of the hidden-activity manifold.
Convex-hull membership is representation-dependent under the nonlinear coordinate changes central to the method.
The paper does not report reconstruction error, independent dimension estimates, geometric preservation, or probe stability.
The bottleneck search is restricted to four powers of two and has no formal plateau criterion.
Only final-hidden-layer activities from simple MNIST and CIFAR-10 MLPs and CNNs are examined.
The architecture sweep conflates accuracy with capacity, depth or width, optimization, and representation geometry.
The same benchmark test sets are reused both to select the claimed dimension plateau and to analyze correctness.
Logistic coefficient z-values are treated as predictor contribution despite collinearity, conditional interaction effects, sample-size sensitivity, and repeated-example dependence.
The Gaussian toy may have full 32D support under its stated isotropic noise, so matching the center-subspace dimension does not validate a true intrinsic-dimension estimator.
Correct-class nearest-neighbor distance requires the true test label and is not an available model-side confidence diagnostic.
No official code, raw results, seeds, checkpoints, hull implementation, or immutable environment is available.
failure_modes: An autoencoder can compress away within-class factors and preserve classification below the manifold's true dimension.
A different nonlinear but equally reconstructive latent reparameterization can flip test points across the training convex hull without changing model predictions.
High latent dimension can make hull feasibility numerically ill-conditioned, and unreported tolerances can change boundary labels.
Distance can predict mistakes because of class overlap, density, margins, or representation clustering even when the prediction rule is not interpolation.
Ground-truth-class distance can produce an artificially strong correctness association because the selected neighbor class is defined by the answer.
Test-set inspection across bottleneck sizes can overstate how sharply a representation dimension was recovered.
Bootstrapping trials while reusing the same test examples can understate uncertainty for population-level conclusions.
Results from poor CIFAR-10 MLPs can reverse or weaken the main distance pattern, as acknowledged in the text and visible in the supplement.
reusable_insights: Separate decision-sufficient bottleneck dimension, reconstruction dimension, and local manifold dimension; they answer different questions.
Before assigning geometric meaning to a latent statistic, state the transformation group under which it is invariant.
Treat latent convex-hull membership as a chart-specific diagnostic unless the chart is fixed or the conclusion is proved invariant.
For proximity-based error analysis, compare distance against density, margin, class ambiguity, and calibrated uncertainty using held-out examples.
Quantify incremental predictor value with cross-validated likelihood, discrimination, calibration, or ablation, not raw z-value magnitude.
Report hull solvers, tolerances, normalization, conditioning diagnostics, and boundary sensitivity whenever convex-hull membership is empirical evidence.
Use independent dimension estimators and probe architectures plus nonlinear synthetic manifolds to test estimator identifiability.
A compact reconstructed code that preserves a frozen classifier is still practically valuable even when it cannot support an intrinsic-geometry claim.
open_questions: Which representation-invariant notion of interpolation can distinguish local reuse from extrapolative computation in a nonlinear network?
How different are classifier-sufficient bottleneck dimension, reconstruction dimension, and local intrinsic dimension on the same hidden activities?
Does the in-hull fraction remain stable across independently trained autoencoders, invertible nonlinear latent warps, and hull tolerances?
Can distance add calibrated predictive value beyond class margin, local density, and standard uncertainty scores on held-out data?
Does an intervention that changes representation distance while preserving labels causally change test correctness?
Do the reported geometry trends hold across layers, residual networks, vision transformers, pretrained models, and genuine distribution shifts?
What clustering and hierarchical resampling scheme correctly handles dependence across examples, model seeds, datasets, and probe seeds?
Can a released implementation reproduce the benchmark hull fractions robustly with an independently specified numerical solver?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning in High Dimension Always Amounts to Extrapolation
competitive_landscape.difference: Balestriero, Pesenti, and LeCun define interpolation by membership in the convex hull of the represented training data and show theoretically and empirically that it becomes exceedingly rare as representation dimension grows. Bonnasse-Gahot directly disputes the operating-regime conclusion by first learning a low-dimensional autoencoder chart. The new result is conditional on that chart and does not invalidate the target paper's dimensional argument; both papers ultimately expose that hull-based terminology is a representation-dependent and weak account of generalization.

competitive_landscape.title: Intrinsic dimension of data representations in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Ansuini and collaborators already report low intrinsic dimension in trained hidden representations, a rise-then-fall layer profile, and correlation between last-layer dimension and test accuracy using dedicated nonlinear dimension estimators. The present paper cites and qualitatively echoes that result; its distinct element is combining a classifier-preserving autoencoder bottleneck with convex-hull and proximity analysis, but that bottleneck is less directly tied to intrinsic-dimension estimation.

competitive_landscape.title: Dimensionality compression and expansion in Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Recanatesi and collaborators independently characterize expansion followed by compression of neural-representation dimension and connect low-dimensional late representations to generalization. Their analysis spans layers and proposes an SGD-noise account, whereas Bonnasse-Gahot probes only the last hidden layer and centers convex hull and nearest-neighbor distance. Consequently the low-dimensional-representation premise and generalization correlation are prior, while the chart-specific interpolation argument is narrower.

competitive_landscape.title: The Intrinsic Dimension of Images and Its Impact on Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Pope and collaborators estimate intrinsic dimension for image datasets, validate estimators with GAN-generated data whose dimension can be manipulated, and test how data dimension affects learning and generalization. That work addresses input-data geometry with explicit estimator validation and public code, while Bonnasse-Gahot studies learned last-layer activities and adds hull/proximity diagnostics. It supplies a stronger precedent for separating estimator validation from downstream task preservation.

competitive_landscape.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
competitive_landscape.difference: Valeriani and collaborators extend intrinsic-dimension and local-neighborhood analysis to large self-supervised protein and image transformers and relate layerwise dimension minima to semantic downstream utility. It has broader architecture and layer coverage and uses a dedicated TwoNN estimator with neighbor-composition analysis. Bonnasse-Gahot predates it and uniquely emphasizes convex-hull interpolation, but does not establish that its final-layer pattern transfers to modern self-supervised models.

competitive_landscape.title: Rethinking Intrinsic Dimension Estimation in Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Schulte and Rügamer theoretically and empirically argue that common neural-representation intrinsic-dimension estimators do not track true underlying dimension and investigate alternative drivers of reported trends. This 2026 AISTATS result directly increases the evidentiary burden for treating a classification-preserving autoencoder width as intrinsic dimension. Bonnasse-Gahot's empirical compression result remains interesting, but its geometric interpretation requires the identifiability and estimator checks highlighted by this later work.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Learning Generalization and the Convex Hull of Training Sets
competitive_landscape.difference: This work evaluates convex-hull membership and decision-boundary extrapolation across pixel, wavelet, and internal representations on MNIST and CIFAR. It is a closer task-and-mechanism predecessor than dimension-only studies and reinforces that hull conclusions depend on the chosen representation.

competitive_landscape.title: Decision boundaries and convex hulls in the feature space that deep learning functions learn from images
competitive_landscape.difference: This pre-paper study analyzes convex hulls and decision boundaries in last-hidden ResNet feature space. It directly precedes the reviewed hidden-representation hull question, while the reviewed work adds an autoencoder chart and distance analysis but provides weaker artifact support.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that common MLPs and CNNs learn low-dimensional final-hidden representations in which most test samples lie inside the training convex hull, so the models actually operate in an interpolation regime; it further claims that better models have lower-dimensional representations and that distance to training examples is a more relevant determinant of correctness than hull membership.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact 20-page arXiv v1 artifact reports a controlled Gaussian demonstration, three-width MLP and three-depth CNN sweeps on MNIST and CIFAR-10, classifier-preserving autoencoder bottlenecks, one main hull/distance figure, and twelve supplementary distance panels. The compact-code and distance-correctness observations are supported within those experiments. Low-dimensional hidden representations and their association with generalization were already established by 2019 work, and the direct 2021 target already argued that hull membership is a poor indicator of generalization. The present artifact has no code or raw data, no hull algorithm, no independent dimension estimator, and no invariance, causal, or out-of-distribution test. Current 2026 work further challenges whether standard neural-representation dimension estimators track true dimension.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a visually clear empirical combination of a frozen-classifier autoencoder probe with convex-hull and nearest-neighbor analysis on simple image classifiers. The strongest reusable result is that a 4- or 8-dimensional reconstructive code can often preserve endpoint classification and that learned-space distance correlates with mistakes. The headline conclusion that the models 'actually' interpolate is not established, because hull membership changes under the same kind of nonlinear representation mapping illustrated by the paper itself. The dimension-generalization claim is also prior and insufficiently isolated. Novelty is therefore narrow and diagnostic rather than a resolution of the interpolation/extrapolation debate.

The archive contains TeX, a compiled BBL, and 72 rendered figure PDFs, but no code, raw results, style file, or BibTeX source.
